claim: Puzzle-shaped cells appear in the epidermis of many plants.
source: The puzzle-shaped cells that appear in the epidermis of many plants are a striking example of a complex cell shape, however their functional benefit has remained elusive.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established observation.

claim: The functional benefit of puzzle-shaped cells has remained elusive.
source: The puzzle-shaped cells that appear in the epidermis of many plants are a striking example of a complex cell shape, however their functional benefit has remained elusive.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Puzzle-shaped cells provide an effective strategy to reduce mechanical stress in the cell wall of the epidermis.
source: We propose that these intricate forms provide an effective strategy to reduce mechanical stress in the cell wall of the epidermis.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors in the abstract.

claim: When tissue-level growth is isotropic, lobes emerge at the cellular level to prevent formation of large isodiametric cells that would bulge under stress produced by turgor pressure.
source: When tissue-level growth is isotropic, we hypothesize that lobes emerge at the cellular level to prevent formation of large isodiametric cells that would bulge under the stress produced by turgor pressure.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Data from various plant organs and species support the relationship between lobes and growth isotropy.
source: Data from various plant organs and species support the relationship between lobes and growth isotropy, which we test with mutants where growth direction is perturbed.
evidence: The authors state that their data supports this relationship.

claim: A mechanism actively regulating cellular stress plausibly reproduces the development of epidermal cell shape.
source: Using simulation models we show that a mechanism actively regulating cellular stress plausibly reproduces the development of epidermal cell shape.
evidence: This is stated as a result from simulation models in the abstract.

claim: Mechanical stress is a key driver of cell-shape morphogenesis.
source: Together, our results suggest that mechanical stress is a key driver of cell-shape morphogenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Plant cells undergo dramatic changes in size and shape during growth and morphogenesis.
source: During growth and morphogenesis, plant cells undergo dramatic changes in size and shape.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cells can expand to over 100 times their original size.
source: Starting from small isodiametric cells in proliferative tissues, cells stop dividing and can expand to over 100 times their original size.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the introduction.

claim: The processes underlying the formation of puzzle cells are presently unclear.
source: The processes underlying the formation of these cells are presently unclear, and it has been proposed that they emerge from either the localized outgrowth of lobes (also called protrusions) (Fu, 2002; Mathur, 2006; Xu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2011), localized restriction of indentations (Fu et al., 2009; Sampathkumar et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2013), or a combination of both (Fu et al., 2005; Abley et al., 2013; Armour et al., 2015; Higaki et al., 2016; Majda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: ROP2 and ROP6 mutually inhibit each other's accumulation at the plasma membrane.
source: ROP2 and ROP6 mutually inhibit each other's accumulation at the plasma membrane, creating a co-repression network that divides the plasma membrane into alternating expression domains, with ROP2 in lobes and ROP6 in indentations (Fu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Fu et al., 2009.

claim: ROP2 is localized in lobes and ROP6 is localized in indentations.
source: ROP2 and ROP6 mutually inhibit each other's accumulation at the plasma membrane, creating a co-repression network that divides the plasma membrane into alternating expression domains, with ROP2 in lobes and ROP6 in indentations (Fu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Fu et al., 2009.

claim: ROP2 recruits actin through RIC4 in the lobes.
source: These proteins are thought to regulate pavement cell interdigitation through their interactions with RIC proteins, with ROP2 recruiting actin through RIC4 in the lobes, and ROP6 recruiting cortical microtubules through RIC1 and katanin to restrict growth in indentations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: ROP6 recruits cortical microtubules through RIC1 and katanin to restrict growth in indentations.
source: These proteins are thought to regulate pavement cell interdigitation through their interactions with RIC proteins, with ROP2 recruiting actin through RIC4 in the lobes, and ROP6 recruiting cortical microtubules through RIC1 and katanin to restrict growth in indentations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Disruptions in the ROP/RIC pathways lead to defects in puzzle cell formation.
source: Disruptions in the ROP/RIC pathways lead to defects in puzzle cell formation (Fu, 2002; Fu et al., 2005; Fu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: A lobe in one cell must be matched by an indentation in its neighbor.
source: Since a lobe in one cell must be matched by an indentation in its neighbor, some manner of extracellular communication is required.
evidence: This is stated as a logical requirement in the introduction.

claim: Auxin has been proposed to act as a signal for extracellular communication in puzzle cell formation.
source: The plant hormone auxin has been proposed to act as this signal (Fu et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2010; Li et al., 2011), although recent data call for a re-evaluation of this hypothesis (Gao et al., 2015; Belteton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Recent data call for a re-evaluation of the hypothesis that auxin acts as a signal for extracellular communication in puzzle cell formation.
source: The plant hormone auxin has been proposed to act as this signal (Fu et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2010; Li et al., 2011), although recent data call for a re-evaluation of this hypothesis (Gao et al., 2015; Belteton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to recent studies.

claim: Turgor pressure in Arabidopsis leaf cells can reach up to 10 bar.
source: Mechanically, plant cells are like small balloons inflated with considerable turgor pressure, up to 10 bar in Arabidopsis leaf cells (Forouzesh et al., 2013), reaching values up to 50 bar in specialized cells such as stomata (Franks et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Forouzesh et al., 2013.

claim: Turgor pressure in specialized cells such as stomata can reach up to 50 bar.
source: Mechanically, plant cells are like small balloons inflated with considerable turgor pressure, up to 10 bar in Arabidopsis leaf cells (Forouzesh et al., 2013), reaching values up to 50 bar in specialized cells such as stomata (Franks et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Franks et al., 2001.

claim: Turgor pressure induces mechanical stress in the cell wall.
source: Turgor pressure induces mechanical stress in the cell wall, which is the ratio of the force acting on a cross-section of the material (cell wall) scaled by the area of the material resisting the force.
evidence: This is stated as a physical principle in the introduction.

claim: For a given turgor pressure, cell size and shape provide a good predictor of mechanical stress if the wall is made of a homogeneous material.
source: If the wall is made of a homogeneous material, then for a given turgor pressure, cell size and shape provide a good predictor of mechanical stress (Niklas, 1992; Geitmann and Ortega, 2009), with larger cells subject to more stress than smaller ones (Bassel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Larger cells are subject to more stress than smaller ones.
source: If the wall is made of a homogeneous material, then for a given turgor pressure, cell size and shape provide a good predictor of mechanical stress (Niklas, 1992; Geitmann and Ortega, 2009), with larger cells subject to more stress than smaller ones (Bassel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Bassel et al., 2014.

claim: The epidermis limits organ growth and is under tension from internal tissues.
source: For epidermal cells composing the outermost cell layer in each organ, minimizing mechanical stress on their walls is likely particularly important as the epidermis limits organ growth and is under tension from internal tissues (Savaldi-Goldstein et al., 2007; Kutschera and Niklas, 2007; Beauzamy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: An increase of cell length in one direction does not significantly increase maximal stress in the cell wall.
source: We observed that an increase of cell length in one direction (50 × 10 × 10 µm) does not significantly increase maximal stress in the cell wall (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Anisotropic growth that results in long thin cells is a mechanically advantageous strategy to limit stress magnitude.
source: This suggests that anisotropic growth that results in long thin cells is a mechanically advantageous strategy to limit stress magnitude, limiting the wall thickness required to maintain the cell's integrity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the simulation results.

claim: A cell expanded in two directions has much higher maximal stress than a cell expanded in one direction.
source: Next, we simulated a cell expanded in two directions (50 × 50 × 10 µm) and observed that the maximal stress was much higher.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations.

claim: Enlarging a cell in two directions creates a large open surface area, causing the cell wall to bulge out in response to turgor pressure, greatly increasing the stress.
source: Enlarging the cell in two directions created a large open surface area, causing the cell wall to bulge out in response to turgor pressure, greatly increasing the stress.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations.

claim: When the third dimension is enlarged to form a cube, only a small increase in maximal stress is observed compared to the 50 × 50 × 10 µm case.
source: When the third dimension is enlarged to form a cube (50 × 50 × 50 µm), only a small increase in maximal stress is observed compared to the 50 × 50 × 10 µm case.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations.

claim: The overall stress is much lower in puzzle-shaped tissue than in simplified cell shape template.
source: While the total and average cell area in the original and simplified tissue is the same, the overall stress is much lower in the original (puzzle-shaped) tissue, especially for large cells (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Adding lobes to a circular cell does not significantly affect stress in the central part of the cell.
source: While stress increases with diameter (Figure 1E), adding lobes to the original cell does not significantly affect stress in the central part of the cell.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Increasing lobe length has no impact on stress in the cell center.
source: Furthermore, increasing lobe length has no impact on stress, although the total volume of the cell increases.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations.

claim: Changing lobe width or number does not affect stress in the cell center.
source: Similarly, changing lobe width or number does not affect stress in the cell center (Figure 1E, inset).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There are stress hot spots located between the protrusions.
source: However, there are stress hot spots located between the protrusions, where values appear to be inversely correlated with the width of the protrusion (the distance between the flanks of two consecutive lobes), and increase with the radius of the central part of the cell.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations.

claim: High stress values appear in open areas and in the indentions between protrusions.
source: In both cases, high stress values appear in open areas and in the indentions between protrusions, consistent with previous observations (Sampathkumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from FEM simulations with a citation to prior work.

claim: The size of the largest empty circle (LEC) that can fit into the cell contour can serve as a proxy for mechanical stress magnitude.
source: Following these observations, we propose that the size of the largest empty circle (LEC) that can fit into the cell contour (Figure 1G, yellow) can serve as a proxy for mechanical stress magnitude in both puzzle and non-puzzle shaped cells.
evidence: This is proposed by the authors based on their FEM simulations.

claim: For long thin cells, the size of the empty circle is the cell diameter, which is known to predict stress for cylindrical cells.
source: For long thin cells, such as in roots or stems, the size of the empty circle is the cell diameter, which is known to predict stress for cylindrical cells (Geitmann and Ortega, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: In a strongly anisotropically growing organ the plant would make long thin cells, whereas in more isotropic organs puzzle cells would be produced.
source: We hypothesize that in a strongly anisotropically growing organ the plant would make long thin cells, whereas in more isotropic organs puzzle cells would be produced.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis by the authors.

claim: It is the requirement for isotropic expansion at the tissue scale that drives the irregular shape of puzzle cells.
source: Counter-intuitively, it is the requirement for isotropic expansion at the tissue scale that drives the irregular shape of puzzle cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion by the authors.

claim: Circularity is not suitable for distinguishing between simple, elongated cells and lobed puzzle cells.
source: However, it is not suitable for our purposes as both simple, elongated cells and lobed puzzle cells have increased circularity values. Consequently, it cannot be used to reliably distinguish between these cell shapes.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the circularity measure.

claim: Cell lobeyness is defined as the perimeter of the cell divided by the perimeter of its convex hull.
source: Here we use a method based on the convex hull (Wu et al., 2016), the smallest convex shape containing the cell (think of a rubber band surrounding the cell). We define cell lobeyness as the perimeter of the cell divided by the perimeter of its convex hull (Figure 1G, white and red, respectively).
evidence: This is stated as the definition of the measure used by the authors.

claim: Cortical microtubules are thought to direct the deposition of cellulose fibrils in the cell wall.
source: Cortical microtubules are thought to direct the deposition of cellulose fibrils in the cell wall (Green, 1962; Paredez et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Cellulose fibrils stiffen the cell wall, causing growth to be favored in the direction perpendicular to the fibrils.
source: These fibrils stiffen the cell wall, causing growth to be favored in the direction perpendicular to the fibrils (Suslov and Verbelen, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Cortical microtubules orient along the maximal direction of tensile stress.
source: Cortical microtubules have also been shown to orient along the maximal direction of tensile stress (Hejnowicz et al., 2000; Hamant et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Predicted stress directions in puzzle cells align with cortical microtubule direction in Arabidopsis cotyledons.
source: This idea is supported by experimental and modeling work showing that predicted stress directions in puzzle cells align with cortical microtubule direction in Arabidopsis cotyledons (Sampathkumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: If tissue growth is isotropic, cells quickly approach their target LEC, and connections representing the cellulose and microtubules begin to stretch.
source: If tissue growth is isotropic, cells quickly approach their target LEC, and connections representing the cellulose and microtubules begin to stretch.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the simulation model.

claim: Lobes emerge as the indentations attract more connections and protrusions lose connections.
source: Lobes emerge as the indentations (concave regions) attract more connections and protrusions (convex regions) lose connections (Figure 2C, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the simulation model shown in Figure 2C and Video 1.

claim: The increased number of connections at indentations is an emergent geometric effect.
source: The increased number of connections at indentations is an emergent geometric effect.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation of the simulation results.

claim: The accumulation of connections in the indentations is consistent with the observed auto-catalytic effect of microtubule bundling in indentations in real pavement cells.
source: Interestingly, the accumulation of connections in the indentations is consistent with the observed auto-catalytic effect of microtubule bundling in indentations in real pavement cells, via induced ROP6/RIC1/katanin-dependent microtubule severing activity (Lin et al., 2013; Sampathkumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: If the simulation is performed with anisotropic growth, the cellulose-microtubule connections are never stretched significantly beyond the LEC, and cells simply elongate, and lobes do not emerge.
source: If the simulation is performed with anisotropic growth, the cellulose-microtubule connections are never stretched significantly beyond the LEC, and cells simply elongate, and lobes do not emerge (Figure 3B,E).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the simulation model shown in Figure 3B,E.

claim: The model is consistent with both the antagonistic local molecular interactions of ROP2-ROP6 and the stress-based feedbacks proposed by Sampathkumar et al. (2014).
source: Thus, although phrased in geometric terms, our model is consistent with both the antagonistic local molecular interactions of ROP2-ROP6 and the stress-based feedbacks proposed by Sampathkumar et al. (2014).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the model with a citation to prior work.

claim: Growing the tissue isotropically produces puzzle-shaped cells that resemble cotyledon epidermal cells.
source: Starting with meristematic-like cells (top), growing the tissue isotropically, i.e. equally in all directions (arrows), produces puzzle-shaped cells (middle) that resemble cotyledon epidermal cells (bottom).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the simulation model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Growing the tissue primarily in one direction (anisotropically) results in elongated cells as observed in the petiole.
source: Growing the tissue primarily in one direction (anisotropically) results in elongated cells (middle) as observed, for example, in the petiole (bottom).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the simulation model shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A gradient of growth anisotropy produces a spatial gradient of cell shapes.
source: A gradient of growth anisotropy (increasing left to right) produces a spatial gradient of cell shapes (middle), as observed between the blade and midrib of a leaf (bottom).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the simulation model shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Similar gradients in cell shape are seen in A. thaliana leaves, where elongated cells cover the anisotropically growing midrib, whereas lobed cells adorn the adjacent isotropically growing leaf blade.
source: Similar gradients in cell shape are seen in A. thaliana leaves, where elongated cells cover the anisotropically growing midrib, whereas lobed cells adorn the adjacent isotropically growing leaf blade (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The emergence of puzzle vs. elongated cells depends only on the anisotropy of growth at the tissue scale when all other model parameters remain constant.
source: To examine the contribution of growth distribution to cell shape we varied growth anisotropy while all other model parameters remained constant (Figure 3A–C). In this case, the emergence of puzzle vs. elongated cells depends only on the anisotropy of growth at the tissue scale, with puzzle cells appearing for isotropic growth, and elongated cells for anisotropic growth (Video 1, Video 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the simulation model shown in Figure 3A-C and Videos 1-2.

claim: When growth is anisotropic, there is no strict 'threshold' for the onset of lobing, but rather it is a continuous characteristic.
source: This exploration showed that when growth is anisotropic, there is no strict 'threshold' for the onset of lobing, but rather it is a continuous characteristic.
evidence: This is stated as a result from parameter space exploration.

claim: The model can generate a diverse range of plausible cell shapes, similar to those observed in nature.
source: Parameter variation also demonstrates that the model can generate a diverse range of plausible cell shapes, similar to those observed in nature (e.g. Figure 3—figure supplement 2B 60% isotropy; which are reminiscent of epidermal cells in maize leaves).
evidence: This is stated as a result from parameter variation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Limiting the size of the LEC by creating lobes during growth reduces the cellular stress.
source: To validate the model, we confirmed in a FEM analysis that limiting the size of the LEC by creating lobes during growth reduces the cellular stress (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is stated as a validation result from FEM analysis shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The maximum stress in simulated tissues plateaus, greatly reducing it compared to isodiametric cells of the same size.
source: This causes the maximum stress in simulated tissues to plateau, greatly reducing it compared to isodiametric cells of the same size (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated as a result from FEM analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The model does not require cell-cell signaling molecules to synchronize the indentations in one cell with the protrusions of its neighbor.
source: The model relies on cell-autonomous mechanical restriction of indentations through controlled cellulose deposition and does not require cell-cell signaling molecules to synchronize the indentations in one cell with the protrusions of its neighbor.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the model.

claim: The model predicts that the signal coordinating ROP6 in the indentation of one cell with ROP2 in the corresponding lobe of the neighboring cell could be passed through the geometry of the cells via its effect on stress patterns or geometry.
source: Although mobile biochemical signals cannot be ruled out (Xu et al., 2010), our model predicts that this signal could be passed through the geometry of the cells via its effect on stress patterns or geometry, with indentations attracting microtubule-cellulose deposition and ROP6, and lobes suppressing microtubules via the cell-autonomous co-repression of ROP2 and ROP6.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model.

claim: Puzzle cells should appear when cells stop dividing and tissue growth is not primarily in one direction.
source: Our model predicts that puzzle cells should appear when cells stop dividing and tissue growth is not primarily in one direction.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model.

claim: The overall growth of cotyledons is isotropic.
source: We used MorphoGraphX (Barbier de Reuille et al., 2015) to extract growth rates and directions, and these results confirm that the overall growth of cotyledons is isotropic as suggested by its round shape.
evidence: This is stated as a result from time-lapse imaging analysis.

claim: There is a significant correlation between growth anisotropy and lobeyness in the isotropically growing cotyledons of Arabidopsis.
source: We then extracted the largest 100 cells from this set (i.e. those most likely to be affected by the stress-minimizing mechanism) and found a significant correlation between growth anisotropy and lobeyness (Pearson correlation coefficient r = −0.46, p=0.6 × 10−6). This supports our hypothesis that growth anisotropy and lobeyness are inversely related in the isotropically growing cotyledons of Arabidopsis (see also Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from time-lapse imaging analysis with statistical support.

claim: The Arabidopsis sepal is an elongated organ with epidermal cells that are either small and relatively isodiametric in shape, or large and elongated.
source: In contrast to cotyledons, the Arabidopsis sepal is an elongated organ with epidermal cells that are either small and relatively isodiametric in shape, or large and elongated.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: Sepals initiate from a band of cells in the floral meristem, undergoing strongly anisotropic growth which produces giant cells that are far less lobed than those of the cotyledon.
source: Sepals initiate from a band of cells in the floral meristem, undergoing strongly anisotropic growth (Hervieux et al., 2016) which produces giant cells that are far less lobed than those of the cotyledon (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation to prior work and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: Growth isotropy and final organ shape correlate with lobeyness in cotyledons and sepals.
source: Thus growth isotropy and final organ shape correlate with lobeyness in these two organs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: Sepals of the ftsh4 mutant show increased variability of organ shape.
source: Sepals of the ftsh4 mutant show increased variability of organ shape (Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: In ftsh4 mutant sepals with more isotropic growth, cells exhibit decreased growth anisotropy and increased lobeyness.
source: In some samples, the growth is more isotropic than wild type, and cells of more isodiametrically shaped organs exhibit decreased growth anisotropy and increased lobeyness, and start to become puzzle shaped (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Overexpressing LONGIFOLIA1 (TRM2, LNG1) gene causes an elongated cell and organ phenotype in A. thaliana cotyledons and leaves.
source: The opposite change in growth anisotropy and organ shape can be seen in plants overexpressing the LONGIFOLIA1 (TRM2, LNG1) gene. This causes an elongated cell and organ phenotype in A. thaliana cotyledons and leaves (Lee et al., 2006; Drevensek et al., 2012), consistent with effects of a related protein in rice grains (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Plants with the elongated p35S::LNG1 phenotype grew more anisotropically than wild type and had epidermal cells with reduced lobeyness.
source: Plants with the elongated phenotype grew more anisotropically than wild type and had epidermal cells with reduced lobeyness (n = 3 time-lapse series for each genotype, Figure 4A–B and F–I).
evidence: This is stated as a result from time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 4A-B and F-I.

claim: The change in growth and organ shape from isodiametric to elongated correlated with a decrease in cell lobeyness in p35S::LNG1 plants.
source: Thus the change in growth and organ shape from isodiametric to elongated correlated with a decrease in cell lobeyness.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: Puzzle-shaped cells were only observed in silicles, not in siliques, in a sample of 21 species from the Brassicaceae family.
source: These fruit pods were either elongated siliques or short, rounded silicles and we only observed puzzle-shaped cells in silicles, not in siliques (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to Figure 4J,K.

claim: The strict correspondence between fruit shape and puzzle-shaped epidermal cells fits the prediction that puzzle shapes are required to allow cells to enlarge in isotropically growing tissues.
source: This strict correspondence between fruit shape and puzzle-shaped epidermal cells fits the prediction of our model that puzzle shapes are required to allow cells to enlarge in isotropically growing tissues, but are not required in elongated organs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: If the cell area increases faster than LEC area, cells must have a mechanism to maintain a low LEC radius.
source: We reasoned that if the cell area increases faster than LEC area, cells must have a mechanism to maintain a low LEC radius.
evidence: This is stated as reasoning for the experiment.

claim: As the cotyledon grows, the ratio of average LEC area to average cell area increases slower than when the cell is circular.
source: Our results show that as the cotyledon grows, the ratio of average LEC area to average cell area increases slower than when the cell is circular.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the time-course imaging analysis.

claim: As organ development progresses, cell area increases faster than LEC area.
source: Consequently, as organ development progresses, cell area increases faster than LEC area, consistent with the idea that increased lobeyness allows surface area to increase faster than the magnitude of stress (Figure 5A, blue signs).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the time-course imaging analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: If stress is a developmental constraint, then when cells grow isotropically without the stress-management mechanism, they should bulge excessively, reach their rupture point and burst.
source: It is commonly observed that the periclinal cell walls slightly bulge out in healthy, turgid cells. However, if stress is indeed a developmental constraint, then when cells grow isotropically without this mechanism, they should bulge excessively, reach their rupture point and burst.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction to test the hypothesis.

claim: The shoot apex of Arabidopsis grows isotropically in areas without lateral organs.
source: The shoot apex of Arabidopsis grows isotropically in areas without lateral organs (Kwiatkowska and Dumais, 2003; Kierzkowski et al., 2012), with the cells presumably managing their mechanical stress by employing cell division to remain small.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: In plants grown with auxin transport inhibitor NPA, the shoot apex is unable to produce lateral organs, and is uniformly covered in small rapidly dividing cells of isodiametric shape.
source: In plants grown with auxin transport inhibitor 1-N-naphtylphtalamic acid (NPA), the shoot apex is unable to produce lateral organs, and is uniformly covered in small rapidly dividing cells of isodiametric shape (Reinhardt et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Treating NPA-grown meristems with oryzalin blocks cell division and anisotropic growth restriction, preventing the formation of puzzle shapes.
source: Treating these meristems with oryzalin, a chemical compound that depolymerizes cortical microtubules, blocks cell division and anisotropic growth restriction, preventing the formation of puzzle shapes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiment.

claim: Oryzalin treatment changes the trajectory of cellulose microfibril-producing molecules (CESA) but does not appear to change the rate of cellulose production.
source: It has been shown in Arabidopsis hypocotyls that oryzalin treatment changes the trajectory of cellulose microfibril-producing molecules (CESA), as there is no organized cortical microtubule array to follow, but does not appear to change the rate of cellulose production (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Cells of shoot apices treated with oryzalin do not divide, but continue to grow developing large, isodiametric shapes that tend to balloon out.
source: Cells of shoot apices in these conditions do not divide, but continue to grow developing large, isodiametric shapes that tend to balloon out (Hamant et al., 2008; Corson et al., 2009; Grandjean, 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Cell bursting was observed in 13 out of 20 samples that displayed full microtubule depolymerization following oryzalin treatment.
source: After treating naked meristems of NPA-grown seedlings with oryzalin (five biological replicates), 20 displayed full microtubule depolymerization following oryzalin treatment (as assessed by the absence of cell division). In those 20 samples, we could see cell bursting in the latest time points of 13 samples, out of which 10 displayed bursting cells located in the flank of the meristem, where cells were substantially larger (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the experiment shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation for cell bursting in the flank of the meristem is that their cell walls could not withstand the increasing mechanical stress induced by the isotropic expansion.
source: Although it cannot be completely excluded that these lateral cells, under these experimental conditions, have different wall properties, the most parsimonious explanation is that their cell walls could not withstand the increasing mechanical stress induced by the isotropic expansion.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Lobe formation in pavement cells is compromised in spike1 (spk1) mutants.
source: Previous reports have shown that lobe formation in pavement cells is compromised in spike1 (spk1) mutants (Qiu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: SPIKE1 protein is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and is required for the production of the active, GTP-bound form of ROP proteins.
source: The SPIKE1 protein is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and is required for the production of the active, GTP-bound form of ROP proteins molecular switches that deliver signals to downstream components.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: SPIKE1 regulates actin polymerization via WAVE and ARP2/3 complexes.
source: SPIKE1 regulates actin polymerization via WAVE and ARP2/3 complexes (Basu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: SPIKE1 activates ROP2, ROP4 and ROP6, thereby promoting isotropic cell expansion.
source: Furthermore, it activates ROP2, ROP4 and ROP6, thereby promoting isotropic cell expansion (Ren et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: spk1 mutant plants have reduced trichome branching, altered organ shape and increased sensitivity to low humidity environments.
source: Mutant plants have a number of severe phenotypes including reduced trichome branching, altered organ shape and increased sensitivity to low humidity environments.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the mutant.

claim: Epidermal cells of spk1 plants have altered shape, with lobes either small or absent.
source: Epidermal cells of spk1 plants have altered shape, with lobes either small or absent, and compared to wild type, their overall cell shape is much less complicated.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: The epidermis of spk1 mutants suffers from defects in cell-cell adhesion, resulting in gaps between cells.
source: Furthermore, the epidermis suffers from defects in cell-cell adhesion, which have been reported to result in gaps between cells that are clearly visible in the cotyledon epidermis from approximately 5 DAG on (Qiu et al., 2002; Ren et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: spk1 cotyledons are narrower, but not longer than wild type cotyledons.
source: It has been reported that spk1 cotyledons are narrower, but not longer than wild type cotyledons (Qiu et al., 2002) and spk1 petals display an increase in growth anisotropy at late stages of development, after the general shape of the organ has been established (Ren et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Epidermal cells of spk1 cotyledons do not have puzzle-shaped forms.
source: In spk1, epidermal cells of the cotyledons do not have puzzle-shaped forms (Figure 5B,D,E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), even though the tissue growth isotropy is similar to wild type plants (n = 3 time-lapse series, Figure 4B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A – cellular growth anisotropy shows a small statistical difference in that spk1 grows more anisotropically than wild type).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to figures.

claim: LEC radius in the final time point is comparable to wild type in spk1 mutant.
source: In our time-lapse experiment, even though lobeyness is greatly reduced in spk1, LEC radius in the final time point is comparable to wild type (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cellular stresses in wild type and spk1 cells are similar and scale with LEC.
source: Our FEM simulations revealed that cellular stresses in wild type and spk1 cells are similar and scale with LEC (compare Figure 1C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result from FEM simulations shown in Figure 1C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell area increases faster than LEC area in spk1 during the course of organ development.
source: We also performed the same analysis as for wild type, imaging spk1 cotyledons 1, 2, 4 and 6 DAG and measuring cell area and LEC area (Figure 5C,D). This revealed a similar trend to that observed in the wild type, with cell area increasing faster than LEC area (Figure 5A) during the course of organ development.
evidence: This is stated as a result from time-course imaging analysis shown in Figure 5A, C, D.

claim: Mean average cell area in spk1 remained similar or lower than in wild type until 6 DAG.
source: At the same time, mean average cell area in spk1 remained similar or lower than in wild type until 6 DAG (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a result from time-course imaging analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Similar LEC size in spk1 mutant and wild type suggests that LEC acts as a threshold for stress based cell shape modification.
source: Similar LEC size in mutant and wild type suggests that LEC acts as a threshold for stress based cell shape modification.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: Instead of forming lobes, the spk1 cells themselves seem to interdigitate generating worm-like shapes.
source: However, instead of forming lobes, the spk1 cells themselves seem to interdigitate generating worm-like shapes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: Holes appear between cells in the growing epidermis of spk1 cotyledons.
source: It is possible that this strategy is insufficient, as holes appear between cells in the growing epidermis of cotyledons (Figure 5E), which may be due to increased mechanical stress.
evidence: This is stated as an observation shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Holes in spk1 cotyledons are more likely to result from direct disruption of the molecular process regulating cellular adhesion rather than increased mechanical stress.
source: However, since holes are already present in cotyledons at 1 DAG it is more likely that they result from direct disruption of the molecular process regulating cellular adhesion, such as actin-driven pectin delivery to cell walls, causing defects prior to the stress-based shape patterning where the final cell shape is established.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The spk1 mutant is unable to make lobes because it fails to activate ROPs which interact with effector proteins to mediate cytoskeletal rearrangements and cell shape.
source: The spk1 mutant is unable to make lobes because it fails to activate ROPs which interact with effector proteins to mediate cytoskeletal rearrangements and cell shape (Basu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Creating interdigitated worm-shaped cells provides an alternate strategy to cover an isotropically growing tissue, although possibly not as efficient in reducing stress as lobe formation.
source: This suggests that creating interdigitated worm-shaped cells provides an alternate strategy to cover an isotropically growing tissue, although possibly not as efficient in reducing stress as lobe formation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: The stress control mechanism is conserved between various organs in A. thaliana, and within the fruit of Brassicaceae.
source: Our data indicates that the stress control mechanism we propose is conserved between various organs in A. thaliana, and within the fruit of Brassicaceae (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data shown in Figure 4J,K.

claim: There was a positive correlation between cell size and lobeyness for each of 19 unrelated plant species.
source: We measured cell area, LEC area and lobeyness in the adaxial epidermis of 19 unrelated plant species including trees, shrubs and herbs. A statistical analysis revealed that there was a positive correlation between cell size and lobeyness for each species (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the multi-species analysis shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Species with the largest average lobeyness also tended to have the largest cells.
source: Species with the largest average lobeyness also tended to have the largest cells (and vice-versa, Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the multi-species analysis shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: When pooling cells of all species together, the Pearson correlation coefficient between lobeyness and cell area was 0.64.
source: When pooling cells of all species together, the Pearson correlation coefficient was 0.64.
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result from the multi-species analysis.

claim: Lobe formation is more likely to be observed in big cells rather than small cells.
source: Lobe formation is therefore more likely to be observed in big cells rather than small cells, which is intuitive if one considers cell division (where cell size remains low) as an alternative strategy to limit LEC size and cell wall stress.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the multi-species analysis results.

claim: The hypothesis that plants create puzzle-shaped cells in order to reduce stress in large isotropically growing cells may be conserved among many plant species.
source: This suggests our hypothesis, that plants create puzzle-shaped cells in order to reduce stress in large isotropically growing cells, may be conserved among many plant species.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the multi-species analysis.

claim: Puzzle shaped cells in the epidermis of many plant species emerge from a mechanism that evolved to limit mechanical stress in tissues that grow isotropically.
source: We propose that the puzzle shaped cells seen in the epidermis of many plant species emerge from a mechanism that evolved to limit mechanical stress in tissues that grow isotropically, such as the epidermis of leaves and cotyledons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: When an epidermal cell becomes large in two directions, stress is greatly increased.
source: FEM analysis of 3D pressurized cells shows that cell shape influences the direction and magnitude of mechanical stress exerted on the cell wall. When an epidermal cell becomes large in two directions (i.e. has a large open area), stress is greatly increased.
evidence: This is stated as a result from FEM analysis.

claim: In stems, roots and siliques, growth is strongly anisotropic, and cells can simply elongate.
source: In stems, roots and siliques, growth is strongly anisotropic, and cells can simply elongate.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: Minimizing mechanical stress by shape regulation may be a way of reducing the resources required to reinforce the cell wall and at the same time maintaining its structural integrity during growth.
source: Since turgor pressure inside cells is high, minimizing mechanical stress by shape regulation may be a way of reducing the resources required to reinforce the cell wall and at the same time maintaining its structural integrity during growth.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: Organs displaying isotropic planar growth have puzzle shaped cells while anisotropically growing organs have more elongated cells with fewer lobes.
source: Organs displaying isotropic planar growth have puzzle shaped cells while anisotropically growing organs have more elongated cells with fewer lobes.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Genetic perturbations that modify growth anisotropy in either direction result in the predicted changes in cell shape.
source: Genetic perturbations that modify growth anisotropy in either direction result in the predicted changes in cell shape.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Isotropic growth at the tissue level is a primary driver of cell shape.
source: Although studies often focus on anisotropic growth at the cellular level when analyzing puzzle cell development (Armour et al., 2015), our hypothesis suggests that isotropic growth at the tissue level is a primary driver of cell shape.
evidence: This is stated as a key point of the hypothesis.

claim: The model explains the gradual emergence of lobed cells from polygons resembling meristematic cells.
source: Our model explains the gradual emergence of lobed cells from polygons resembling meristematic cells, providing an explanation for the till now enigmatic morphogenesis of these distinctive cells.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the model.

claim: The model suggests that the main driver of the complex puzzle shape comes from the restriction of growth in the indentations, rather than the promotion of growth in the protrusions.
source: The model suggests that the main driver of the complex puzzle shape comes from the restriction of growth in the indentations, rather than the promotion of growth in the protrusions.
evidence: This is stated as a key insight from the model.

claim: The model predicts that the puzzle cell shape is triggered by isotropic growth.
source: It also predicts that the puzzle cell shape is triggered by isotropic growth, and that puzzle cell morphogenesis may not require any signaling molecules to coordinate a protrusion in one cell with the corresponding indentation of its neighbor.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model.

claim: The mechanism predicts that spatial differences in cell wall material properties, corresponding to lobes and indentations, should appear in periclinal cell walls as organized cellulose distributions appear.
source: The mechanism also predicts that spatial differences in cell wall material properties, corresponding to lobes and indentations, should appear in periclinal cell walls as organized cellulose distributions appear, consistent with observations that cellulose-bundles accumulate in high-stress indentations (Sampathkumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the mechanism with a citation to prior work.

claim: Spatial differences in stiffness corresponding to incipient lobes and indentations have recently been measured in cross-sections of anticlinal cell walls.
source: Spatial differences in stiffness corresponding to incipient lobes and indentations have recently been measured in cross-sections of anticlinal cell walls (Majda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: The model is consistent with the functions attributed to the main molecular players that have been reported to influence puzzle cell formation, the ROP family of GTP-ases.
source: Our model is also consistent with the functions attributed to the main molecular players that have been reported to influence puzzle cell formation, the ROP family of GTP-ases.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the model.

claim: On the convex side (protrusion), ROP2 and ROP4 inactivate the microtubule-associated protein RIC1, thereby suppressing the formation of microtubule arrays, and activate RIC4 which enhances the assembly of actin microfibrils.
source: On the convex side (protrusion), ROP2 and ROP4 inactivate the microtubule-associated protein RIC1, thereby suppressing the formation of microtubule arrays, and activate RIC4 which enhances the assembly of actin microfibrils. This was proposed to result in growth promotion (Fu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: On the concave side (indentation), ROP6 activates RIC1 and katanin, promoting the formation of bundled microtubule arrays that restrict growth.
source: On the concave side (indentation), ROP6 activates RIC1 and katanin, promoting the formation of bundled microtubule arrays that restrict growth (Fu et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The model is consistent with the idea that ROP6 is a part of the stress sensing mechanism, and that stress (or strain) is the trigger for localized ROP6 accumulation.
source: Nonetheless, our model is also consistent with the idea that ROP6 is a part of the stress sensing mechanism, and that stress (or strain) is the trigger for localized ROP6 accumulation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the model.

claim: The molecular mechanism for how stress (or strain) could be sensed and its relationship to the ROPs is currently unknown.
source: Currently, the molecular mechanism for how stress (or strain) could be sensed and its relationship to the ROPs is unknown, although microtubules have been proposed to respond to stress in planta (Hejnowicz et al., 2000; Hamant et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: A curvature sensing mechanism could be involved in stress sensing.
source: Since stress is closely related to shape in pressurized plant cells, a curvature sensing mechanism could be involved (Higaki et al., 2016), similar to that proposed for villi patterning during gut morphogenesis (Shyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations to prior work.

claim: A ROP2-ROP6 co-repression network can partition a cell in discrete domains of ROP2 and ROP6 expression.
source: Simulations have shown that a ROP2-ROP6 co-repression network can indeed partition a cell in discrete domains of ROP2 and ROP6 expression (Abley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: The intracellular partitioning network works in concert with a mechanical or geometric signal, transmitted by the shape of the cell itself.
source: Our data suggest that this intracellular partitioning network works in concert with a mechanical or geometric signal, transmitted by the shape of the cell itself.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data.
